### Introduction

You've just been hired as a junior data scientist at TechStart Analytics, a
consulting firm for early-stage companies. Your first client is **CloudFit**, a
fitness app. Its CEO, Sarah, wants to understand how people use the app and,
above all, **which users will cancel after their free trial**.

This problem set covers statistical learning, linear regression,
classification, logistic regression, K-nearest neighbors, and
cross-validation (Days 9–14). It is **conceptual**: you won't fit any models.
Instead, you'll read output that CloudFit's analysts already produced and
explain what it means, the same skill the exams test. It should take about
**75 minutes**.

### Instructions

* This problem set is mostly reading tables and output. To see them formatted
  while you work, switch RStudio to **Visual** mode: click **Visual** at the top
  left of the editor (next to **Source**), or press Ctrl+Shift+F4
  (Cmd+Shift+F4 on a Mac). Click **Source** to switch back.
* Write your answers in the space after each question. Short-answer questions
  want 2–4 sentences, not an essay.
* Use the R chunks as a calculator wherever a question asks for a number, so
  your work is visible. Show the formula, not just the result.
* Knit this document before submitting. It should knit without errors, and your
  `.md` output must be visible on GitHub. If I can't see your output, I can't
  grade it.

### The data

CloudFit's user records include:

| Variable | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `age` | user's age, 18–64 |
| `workouts` | workouts logged per week, 0–7 |
| `premium` | number of premium features the user has tried, 0–6 |
| `app_minutes` | average minutes per day spent in the app |
| `churn` | `Yes` if the user **cancelled** after the free trial, `No` if they renewed |

## Part 1: The Big Picture (12 minutes)

### Question 1.1: What kind of problem is it?

Sarah has four questions. For each one, say whether it is **supervised** or
**unsupervised**. If it's supervised, also say whether it is **regression** or
**classification**, and whether the main goal is **prediction** or
**inference**. One sentence of reasoning each.

a) "Which of this week's free-trial users are going to cancel?"

b) "If we get a user to do one more workout a week, how many more minutes a day
   will they spend in the app?"

c) "Are there natural groups of users with similar habits?"

d) "How many minutes a day will a brand-new user spend in the app?"

*Your answers:*

### Question 1.2: How flexible should the model be?

A previous intern tried to predict `app_minutes` from `age` alone. The intern
drew a random training set of 60 users, fit polynomials in `age` of different
degrees, and measured the MSE on 2,000 other users, then repeated this for 200
different training sets and summarized the results. (Degree 0 means predicting the
average for everyone.)

| Degree | Training MSE (average) | Test MSE (median) |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 467 | 470 |
| 1 | 461 | 476 |
| 2 | 419 | 447 |
| 4 | 405 | 464 |
| 8 | 377 | 508 |

(The test column reports the median because a few degree-8 fits produced wild
predictions that would swamp an average. That is itself a sign of high
variance.)

a) Training MSE falls every time the degree rises. Explain why it has to.

b) Which degree would you recommend, and why?

c) Compare degree 2 and degree 8. Which has more **bias**? Which has more
   **variance**? Explain what would happen to each fitted curve if the intern
   drew a different set of 60 users.

d) The straight line (degree 1) predicts new users **worse** than just guessing
   the average (degree 0). Degree 2 does better than both. What does that tell
   you about the shape of the relationship between age and app minutes?
   Sketch it in words.

*Your answers:*

(`Yes`)**.

### Question 4.2: Choosing K

The analyst also tried KNN on the same 4,000 training and 1,000 test users,
using all four predictors:

| K | Training error rate | Test error rate |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.0% | 31.4% |
| 5 | 18.6% | 25.9% |
| 25 | 21.1% | 22.8% |
| 100 | 22.6% | 22.2% |
| 300 | 22.7% | 23.3% |

a) Why is the training error rate **exactly** 0 when K = 1?

b) On the test set, 27.1% of users cancel. Compare K = 1's test error rate to
   the predict-nobody-cancels baseline. What does that tell you?

c) Which K would you choose? As K rises from 1 to 300, describe what happens to
   bias and to variance.

d) Before running KNN, the analyst **standardized** all four predictors. Why?
   If they hadn't, which predictor(s) would mostly decide who counts as a

## Part 5: Cross-Validation (10 minutes)

To compare models fairly, the analyst ran **5-fold cross-validation** on all
5,000 users (cutoff 0.5 throughout):

| Model | Mean CV error rate | SD across folds | Mean CV F1 | SD across folds |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Logistic regression | 23.1% | 1.3% | 0.50 | 0.05 |
| KNN, K = 5 | 25.5% | 1.3% | 0.48 | 0.03 |
| KNN, K = 25 | 23.2% | 0.7% | 0.49 | 0.03 |

a) In Part 3, the model was scored on a single split: 4,000 training users and
   1,000 test users. What does 5-fold cross-validation do differently, and
   why is it a more trustworthy comparison?

b) Logistic regression and KNN with K = 25 differ by 0.1 percentage points in
   mean error rate. Is that a meaningful difference? Use the SD column.

c) Which model would you recommend to Sarah? Give one reason that isn't about
   the error rate.
